video_title: Could we use Trump's tricks to make good green policy?
gist: Roosevelt Institute's Todd Tucker argues that the emergency and state-capitalist tools Trump has pioneered — Defense Production Act preemption of state law, federal equity stakes like the 10% of Intel, the US Steel golden share, sovereign wealth funds — are precedents a 2029 Democratic administration should seize for grid buildout, green steel and EVs rather than dismantle. He and host David Roberts spar over whether the political system will treat progressive use of those tools symmetrically, and Tucker names filibuster reform and a more aggressive posture toward the Supreme Court as day-one preconditions for any serious climate agenda.

themes.theme: DPA preemption as a clean-energy weapon

insights.claim: Oil company Sable petitioned the Trump administration to invoke the Defense Production Act to force restart of a ruptured California offshore pipeline, and a federal judge ruled the DPA can override state law and regulation — a precedent now headed to the Ninth Circuit.
insights.speaker: David Roberts (host)
insights.so_what: A Ninth Circuit affirmation would make federal DPA orders a general-purpose override of state permitting and environmental law, materially changing siting risk for both fossil and clean infrastructure.

insights.claim: The same DPA authority used to preempt California law for oil could be used by a future administration to seize rights of way and build out the electrical grid, and to fix supply-chain failures of the kind that broke offshore wind projects around 2023.
insights.speaker: Todd Tucker
insights.so_what: If this becomes doctrine, transmission and offshore wind developers gain a federal route around state blockage — a step-change in project risk for grid and wind buildout.
insights.quote: If Trump can use the defense production act to preempt California zoning law, then the next administration could do so to get the right of way to build out the electrical grid.

insights.claim: Tucker's brief on the Sable episode concluded the DPA should not be repealed but should be used just as aggressively by a future administration to push geothermal and offshore wind past state permitting, reallocate electricity away from data centers that aren't paying their way, and preempt state right-to-work laws.
insights.speaker: David Roberts (host)
insights.so_what: Names three concrete targets — geothermal/wind permitting, data-center load allocation, and labor law — where a future federal emergency order could reprice risk fast.

insights.claim: Tucker's core asymmetry argument is that right-wing governments use emergency powers to the hilt while progressive governments hold back in the name of outdated norms, and that this restraint must end.
insights.speaker: Todd Tucker
insights.so_what: A norms-abandonment posture on the left implies far higher policy volatility across administrations — a durable risk premium on regulated energy assets.
insights.quote: we need to get rid of this asymmetry where, you know, right-wing anti-climate governments use their powers to the hilt. But when progressive governments are in power, they sort of hold themselves back

insights.claim: Roberts's central pushback is that policy tools are not politically agnostic: courts, media and the public will react very differently when Democrats use emergency powers for radical reform than when Republicans use them to defend incumbents.
insights.speaker: David Roberts (host)
insights.so_what: Cuts against the whole 'inherit Trump's tools' thesis — expect the legal and media reception, not the statute, to determine whether these precedents actually transfer.
insights.quote: just because the tool is the same doesn't mean the two sides will be doing the same thing or will be treated the same way

insights.claim: Tucker predicts as a matter of forecasting, not preference, that the next administration will keep Trump's equity stakes and tariffs rather than unwind them, and will repurpose them for climate priorities — as Biden did by keeping and extending Trump's China tariffs including on Chinese EVs.
insights.speaker: Todd Tucker
insights.so_what: Base case for 2029: no unwind of federal equity stakes or tariffs — position for continuity of state intervention, not reversion to laissez-faire.
insights.quote: I predict that the next administration will come in and find ways to use these tools to its own advantage and for purposes like climate policy.

themes.theme: What Biden-era policy actually taught about durability

insights.claim: Most Biden-era clean energy tax credits survived the 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act despite repeal being a top Trump campaign priority — everything except the wind and solar credits stayed, with fade-outs for mature sectors and continuing support for hydrogen, geothermal and other infant industries.
insights.speaker: Todd Tucker
insights.so_what: Tax-credit durability is far higher than the post-2024 doomer consensus assumed — hydrogen and geothermal developers retain federal support that wind and solar have lost.
insights.quote: all the tax credits except for the wind and solar tech

insights.claim: The Biden model took roughly two years (2021-2022) to pass the legislation and another one to two years to write implementing regulations and move money — too slow for voters to see benefits inside a four-year term.
insights.speaker: Todd Tucker
insights.so_what: Speed-to-visible-benefit is the binding political constraint; the next wave of policy will favor executive tools that disburse fast over legislated programs that don't.
insights.quote: that is not fast enough as it turns out in our democracy in the 2020s

insights.claim: A 2029 administration will have to execute faster with far less capacity, because federal agencies have lost up to 30% or more of their staff under Musk and DOGE.
insights.speaker: Todd Tucker
insights.so_what: Administrative capacity is now the scarce input — favors blunt instruments (equity stakes, emergency orders, public ownership) over grant programs requiring staff to administer.
insights.quote: Depending on the agency of the federal government, we've lost up to 30% or more of the staff.

insights.claim: Biden lawyers spent years trying to Supreme Court-proof regulations, which is a major reason implementation was slow; Tucker argues the next administration should stop second-guessing John Roberts and optimize for policy and political return instead.
insights.speaker: Todd Tucker
insights.so_what: Implies faster, legally riskier rulemaking after 2029 — more policy issued quickly, more of it later vacated, higher regulatory whipsaw for energy investors.
insights.quote: rather than spend two years trying to second guessess what John Roberts is going to do, you can just acknowledge that they're completely political actors

insights.claim: Project 2025 has already had over 50% of its recommendations implemented as of earlier this year according to the Center for Progressive Reform, but the asymmetry is that destroying and repealing is far easier and faster than building and passing.
insights.speaker: Todd Tucker
insights.so_what: A pre-written build agenda will convert to policy far more slowly than a demolition agenda did — discount the pace of any 2029 green restoration accordingly.
insights.quote: implemented as of earlier this year over 50% of the recommendations

themes.theme: Filibuster and court reform as day-one preconditions

insights.claim: Tucker puts filibuster reform on day one of a 2029 agenda, arguing that even a movement caring only about emissions or clean energy must embrace it because Senate malapportionment structurally favors fossil-fuel states.
insights.speaker: Todd Tucker
insights.so_what: Filibuster abolition is the single gate on whether 2029 produces statutory climate policy or another round of reversible executive orders.
insights.quote: I say it has to be, you know, day one.

insights.claim: A resident of Wyoming has roughly 70 times the Senate voting power of a Californian, and climate-driven demographic resettlement is projected to make that malapportionment gap twice as bad by 2100.
insights.speaker: Todd Tucker
insights.so_what: Quantifies a structurally worsening headwind for federal climate legislation — a reason to weight state, municipal and executive channels over Congress in long-horizon scenarios.
insights.quote: they have about 70 times as much power as someone from California

insights.claim: The 'everything bagel' critique of Biden policy is misdirected: labor and childcare conditions were bolted onto semiconductor and clean energy subsidies precisely because filibuster and reconciliation rules made direct labor law reform like the PRO Act impossible.
insights.speaker: Todd Tucker and David Roberts
insights.so_what: Predicts that if the filibuster falls, subsidy programs get cleaner and less conditional — better economics for manufacturers taking federal money.
insights.quote: part of the reason that you had to do that was because of the filibuster and reconciliation rules, which make it impossible to do labor law reform in a more sane way

insights.claim: Adding justices is the only near-term Supreme Court reform achievable by statute, but risks tit-for-tat escalation; the better structural fixes — ending life tenure, rotating lower-court judges onto the Court — all require constitutional amendments ratified by disproportionately small-state legislatures.
insights.speaker: Todd Tucker
insights.so_what: Means court composition stays a live political risk indefinitely; no durable legal shelter for climate regulation is coming this decade.
insights.quote: Democrats add 10 justices and then Republicans that add 20 and then, you know, before you know it, you just kind of have a hundred justices.

insights.claim: Tim Meyer's proposed grand bargain — a president uses expansive executive authorities fast, then trades statutory limits on those powers for Congress codifying the policy — is greeted skeptically by Roberts, who doubts any president would voluntarily surrender newly acquired power.
insights.speaker: David Roberts (host)
insights.so_what: If executive aggrandizement is a ratchet, energy policy stays hostage to four-year swings regardless of which party wins — the durability premise of the whole project is in doubt.

insights.claim: Nam and Driscoll argue the US should accept that it is a consumption-oriented service economy, buy cheap Chinese green hardware, and build the green coalition around building trades, utilities, grid, software, installation and financing rather than around factories.
insights.speaker: David Roberts (host), summarizing Nam and Driscoll
insights.so_what: A live intellectual current that would drop tariffs and localization mandates in favor of deployment volume — bullish for installers, EPCs and grid services, bearish for domestic panel manufacturers.
insights.quote: China's doing us a favor. They're manufacturing a bunch of cheap green stuff.

insights.claim: The growth-model framework holds that countries are path-dependently either consumption- or production-oriented, and Trump's tariffs demonstrate the constraint: taxing imports in a consumption economy drives inflation up and makes the tariffs politically unsustainable rather than magically producing factories.
insights.speaker: Todd Tucker
insights.so_what: Implies tariff levels are politically unstable at high inflation — a mean-reversion case on protection for import-dependent green supply chains.
insights.quote: if you put a bunch of tariffs on all the stuff we import, inflation's going to go through the roof, and it's going to be really hard to keep those tariffs in place

insights.claim: Joel Dodge's counter-proposal is that the federal government stop trying to lure private manufacturing and instead build, own and operate its own factories on the WWII munitions model, since removing Wall Street's demand for super profits makes domestic production viable where private capital says it isn't.
insights.speaker: David Roberts (host), summarizing Joel Dodge
insights.so_what: Public factories would compete with, not subsidize, private manufacturers in targeted supply chains — a tail risk and an opportunity depending on which segment you own.
insights.quote: if you take out the need to get super profits like Wall Street demands, then you can actually do some of this manufacturing here even if it wouldn't be economical on a purely privatrun capitalist equation

insights.claim: Roberts argues the value capture debate is miscast because the vast majority of a solar panel's value accrues over 20 to 30 years of cheap electricity to the owner and installer, not to the manufacturer.
insights.speaker: David Roberts (host)
insights.so_what: Reframes cheap Chinese imports as a domestic value-creation input — the analytical case for deployment-maximizing rather than protectionist policy.
insights.quote: the vast majority of the value of the panel is going to come from 20 to 30 years of cheap electricity

insights.claim: Tucker's counter is that manufacturing is an ecosystem, so ceding solar panels also costs the upstream and downstream capabilities that feed other manufacturing processes; a new cost-benefit analysis would likely write off solar permanently while defending cutting-edge sectors.
insights.speaker: Todd Tucker
insights.so_what: Suggests future US industrial policy triages by sector — expect support to concentrate in frontier technologies and abandon commodity solar entirely.
insights.quote: once you start giving up parts of your manufacturing ecosystem to another country that it doesn't just stop at the solar panels

themes.theme: State capitalism: equity stakes vs. golden shares

insights.claim: The US government now owns 10% of Intel, a stake Tucker says almost no one in the public is aware of, alongside tens of billions in equity stakes across semiconductors and upstart rare earth companies.
insights.speaker: Todd Tucker
insights.so_what: Federal shareholding is now a standing feature of US equity markets — governance, disclosure and political risk for these names are permanently altered.
insights.quote: we now own 10% of Intel, the American public does. That's a pretty big deal. That's worth a lot of money.

insights.claim: The Intel deal is structurally weak for the public: the government contractually agreed to defer to company management on any important topic and dropped Biden-era domestic reinvestment requirements, trading away control in exchange for ownership.
insights.speaker: Todd Tucker
insights.so_what: Investors should not price the federal stake as a governance overhang at Intel — it is passive by contract, unlike the US Steel arrangement.
insights.quote: we've kind of gotten rid of the control that we had under Biden in exchange for more ownership

insights.claim: The US Steel golden share cost the government nothing and returns nothing, but confers a federal veto over ten categories of corporate decision-making from the company name and Pittsburgh headquarters to actual factory investment plans — maximum control with zero ownership.
insights.speaker: Todd Tucker
insights.so_what: The golden share is the cheapest, most replicable instrument of state control — expect it to be the template for future federal intervention in strategic firms.
insights.quote: we do have a federal veto over 10 different categories of corporate decision-making, ranging from changing their name to being based in Pittsburgh to like actual investment plans for a lot of their factories

insights.claim: A golden share in US Steel during the Biden years could have directed the company to reline its facilities for green steel instead of coal and natural gas, and Tucker argues day-to-day board-level supervision is superior to thousand-page grant and loan agreements.
insights.speaker: Todd Tucker
insights.so_what: Steel decarbonization hinges on a handful of relining decisions at a half dozen facilities — a small set of capital events with outsized emissions and policy consequences.
insights.quote: we need you to go down the decarbonization path, and by the way, we'll give you some subsidies and other support, but we're also, as a board member of this company, going to be instructing you to do that

insights.claim: Obama's 2009 GM and Chrysler stakes were deliberately timely, temporary and targeted with no attempt to steer management, and Tucker argues that using that leverage to force an EV transition would have produced a completely different 20-year trajectory for the US auto industry.
insights.speaker: Todd Tucker
insights.so_what: Establishes the template a 2029 administration would apply to any future auto bailout — conditionality on electrification rather than a quick exit.
insights.quote: We would have had a completely different trajectory over the last 20 years had Obama used his leverage in the way that Trump is doing.

themes.theme: Utilities, states and the permitting blind spot

insights.claim: Shelley Welton argues the industrial policy revival has strangely ignored public utility law, even though utilities are a huge, decarbonization-critical industry over which the public already holds considerable control that goes unused.
insights.speaker: David Roberts (host), summarizing Shelley Welton
insights.so_what: Existing utility regulatory authority is the lowest-friction lever for accelerating clean buildout — no new statute required, which is why it may move first.

insights.claim: Publicly owned utilities have been boxed into mirroring private sector practice, but Tucker says nothing in their law or governing documents prevents them from prioritizing faster clean energy buildout, reviving progressive-era 'networks, platforms and utilities' thinking as regional economic planning.
insights.speaker: Todd Tucker
insights.so_what: Watch public power authorities and municipal utilities as the venue where clean-buildout mandates appear without needing Congress or the courts.
insights.quote: there's not any reason in the law or in the governing documents that would keep them from prioritizing more buildout, quicker buildout of clean energy

insights.claim: The largest existing federal public utility, TVA, is currently heading toward more fossil fuels — a live counterexample showing public ownership does not automatically produce decarbonization.
insights.speaker: David Roberts (host)
insights.so_what: Public ownership is a lever whose direction depends entirely on who holds it — a caution against treating state capitalism as inherently green.
insights.quote: the public utilities we do have, TVA is hurting in the direction of more fossil fuels

insights.claim: The Roosevelt collection contains no chapter on permitting reform, interconnection queues or transportation, which Tucker attributes to optimism that bipartisan permitting legislation will be resolved before 2029 — an omission he concedes he would fix.
insights.speaker: Todd Tucker
insights.so_what: A leading progressive shop is betting permitting gets solved on a bipartisan basis in this Congress — a testable near-term prediction for grid buildout timelines.

insights.claim: Roberts argues permitting reform deserves priority even on a pure power-analysis basis, because unblocking interconnection and transmission would build so much clean energy that it changes facts on the ground and shifts the political economy in favor of further reform.
insights.speaker: David Roberts (host)
insights.so_what: Frames deployment volume itself as the durability mechanism — a reason to weight installed-capacity milestones over legislative wins when forecasting policy persistence.

themes.theme: Abundance, affordability and theory of power

insights.claim: Tucker's critique is that abundance and affordability politics are thin programs with no theory of power — useful diagnostics of regulatory accretion, but lacking any account of how to build the political movement that would carry them out.
insights.speaker: Todd Tucker
insights.so_what: Signals that the emerging Democratic energy agenda will fuse deregulation-for-speed with an explicitly class-based coalition strategy rather than adopting abundance on its own terms.
insights.quote: thin thin programs with no theory of power

insights.claim: Municipal 'sewer socialists' are already absorbing abundance ideas about cutting red tape because they believe fast visible results raise the political yield to workers' rights movements and their broader coalition.
insights.speaker: Todd Tucker
insights.so_what: The left-municipal fusion of deregulation plus labor mobilization is the model most likely to be scaled federally in 2029.
insights.quote: sewer socialists at the municipal level that are wholly embracing some of the ideas that the abundance movement talks about in terms of getting rid of red tape

insights.claim: Tucker's structural objection to affordability politics is that prices and wages are two sides of the same variable — the fastest way to cut prices is to abolish the minimum wage, which nobody thinks is good policy.
insights.speaker: Todd Tucker
insights.so_what: A warning that cost-of-living framing alone can be captured by wage suppression; expect progressive energy affordability arguments to be paired with labor standards.
insights.quote: one very easy way to bring prices down real quick is to get rid of the minimum wage, right? And pay people tiny amounts

insights.claim: Tucker challenges the conventional wisdom that a new administration can only accomplish one or two big things per term, arguing that progressive city administrations doing new things every week show the constraint is soft if paired with a mobilization strategy.
insights.speaker: Todd Tucker
insights.so_what: If true, forecasts of a narrow 2029 legislative window may understate the volume of policy change; if false, expect the agenda to collapse to filibuster reform plus one bill.
insights.quote: it's not a hard and fast rule of physics that we can't be doing more
